caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and snippets; verify before outreach.
Several linkedin urls were copied from meetup event pages where the organiser linked the speaker, not from search results; each such person has a note saying so.
Titles marked "(title not stated)" are placeholders; the source named the employer but not the role.
The 2025-12-04 chapter entry appears to be the joint snowflake user group evening at telenet.
No named speakers were found for pyladies brussels, r-ladies brussels or wids belgium talks, so the women-in-data pool is only four wids belgium ambassadors.
Job-ad coverage is thin: stepstone and aijobs pages were empty or redirected.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.

caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages/snippets and are often inferred from the employer's HQ — verify before outreach.
Only public professional information is recorded; no personal contact details. Pronouns only when self-stated.
Most people come from other London meetups' line-ups, so proven speakers far outnumber emerging voices; the emerging voices are concentrated at Monzo and The Information Lab (the chapter's host).
Talks from 2022-2023 list the employer at the time; several of those people have since moved.
Seven Information Lab people are listed; the chapter is hosted there, so weigh them against outside speakers for line-up balance.

LinkedIn: 3 of 121 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 118 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.

chapters.label: Vilnius
caveats: Titles come from search snippets and may be stale — verify profiles before reaching out.
CV-Online and CVMarket keyword search only match titles, so they returned no dbt results.
Duplicate postings (same role in Vilnius and Kaunas) are listed separately.
Meetup.com attendee lists need a login, so past attendees are not included. The group has 188 members.
The session's web-search cap was reached, so Nord Security/Kilo/Oxylabs internal tech talks, OxyCon, GDG Vilnius and university events were not fully covered.
Several strong speakers (Augustinas Karvelis, Mantas Satkevičius, Marius Žukauskas) have no confirmed LinkedIn URL; find them via their company pages.

Emerging-voice yield in Lithuania is low: search engines rarely link Medium/dev.to/Substack authors or LinkedIn posts to Lithuania, and no dbt engineering-blog posts were found at Kilo Health, Nord Security, Surfshark, Hostinger, Oxylabs, TransferGo, Eneba or PVcase. Asking the meetup's own channels (dbt Slack #local-baltics, the Meetup group) for volunteers may find more first-time speakers than search.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Job ads were read on 2026-10-01. Ads close, so check the link before quoting one.

caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages/snippets and are often inferred from the employer's HQ; verify before outreach.
Only public professional information is recorded; no personal contact details. Pronouns only when self-stated.
dbt Summit 2026 talks are linked to the overview blog post, not the session page; speaker titles were not on the overview.
Fivetran and dbt Labs have merged; decide whether Fivetran and Census staff (Toby Mao, Donny Flynn) fall under the dbt Labs outreach exclusion.
Several leads come from customer quotes (featured) and need a talk ask rather than a re-invite.

LinkedIn: 7 of 76 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 69 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Women-in-data community speakers are recorded from event pages; employers are as stated on the event date and may be out of date.

caveats: Titles and employers of past speakers come from the meetup talk text; verify before outreach.
Speakers found through local groups have an unverified location: a talk at a local event does not show where someone lives.
Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and snippets; verify before outreach.
Two of the four Medellín job ads were closed when fetched (Sprocket, Salt), so they show demand but not open roles.
No first-time speakers were found: no Medellín author with public dbt content surfaced in about 20 calls.

chapters.label: Kuala Lumpur
caveats: Titles and employers come from public pages/snippets and may be stale — verify before outreach.
Only public professional information is recorded; no personal contact details.

Very few Malaysia-based people have public dbt content. Most speaker leads are data leads at companies whose job ads require dbt (Ryt Bank, GXBank, foodpanda, Funding Societies); ask them for a dbt talk rather than assuming one exists.
LinkedIn URLs were matched from search snippets only; people with linkedin_confidence 'not_searched' still need a check.
freehire.me dbt tags come from automatic extraction; open the ad before treating dbt as core.
Speaker names for Snowflake World Tour sessions come from LinkedIn post snippets, not the agenda page.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Employers and dbt wording come from public job ads on 2026-10-01; ads close, so check the employer before outreach.
Some freehire.me ads are tagged Malaysia but are for other countries; ads placed in Singapore, Karachi, Dubai or written in Danish were left out.
Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and snippets. Verify before outreach.
Only two new people were found in about 30 calls. Neither is a first-time speaker, and neither has a relevant dbt-style talk.
Talk dates for Data Council Talks #10 and #11 are not shown on the event pages.

chapters.label: Melbourne
caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages/snippets and are often inferred from the employer's HQ — verify before outreach.
Only public professional information is recorded; no personal contact details. Pronouns only when self-stated.

LinkedIn: 12 of 56 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 44 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Employers and dbt wording come from public job ads on 2026-10-01; ads close, so check the employer before outreach.
Recruiter ads rarely name the client. A role listed under a recruiter does not show which company uses dbt.
Ads placed only as Victoria are assumed to be in Greater Melbourne unless the text says otherwise.

chapters.label: Seoul
caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and listings; verify before outreach.
Korean names are romanised by the researcher in family-name-first order unless the person shows their own romanisation; check spelling with the person.
Many speakers from Airflow Korea and Snowflake Korea listings show no employer; they sit under 'Independent / no company' until verified.
Women-in-data sourcing is thin: PyLadies Seoul is the only active women-in-tech data community found, and its talks are Python and analysis rather than dbt.
Job ads were read on 2026-10-01; wanted.co.kr does not expose posting dates in the fields read.

LinkedIn: 1 of 59 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 58 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Several community hosts are known only by a Meetup first name or handle; confirm full names before outreach.
Job ads were read on 2026-10-01. Ads close, so check the link before quoting one.

chapters.label: Singapore
caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages/snippets and are often inferred from the employer's HQ - verify before outreach.
Only public professional information is recorded; no personal contact details. Pronouns only when self-stated.
Very few Singapore people publish about dbt. Most leads here are data engineers who spoke about pipelines, data mesh or semantic layers; ask each whether they use dbt.
The emerging-voice rule raises Grab and foodpanda blog authors to tier 1 even though their posts do not mention dbt; treat them as first-time speakers on a data topic.

Gender was not inferred. The GovTech STACK series has many speakers who may help balance a line-up; confirm with organisers who know them. PyLadies Singapore and Women Devs SG are the women-in-tech communities found.
The web-search budget ran out after about 12 searches, so Coalesce/dbt Summit speaker lists, Databricks and Snowflake World Tour Singapore agendas, and LinkedIn were not covered.

LinkedIn: 9 of 82 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 73 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers and organisers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke or organised (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Employers and dbt wording come from public job ads on 2026-10-01; ads close, so check the employer before outreach.
Recruiter ads rarely name the client. A role listed under a recruiter does not show which company uses dbt.
A remote ad, an ad in French and ads where DBT means something else (digital business transformation) were left out.

chapters.label: Taipei
caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and posts and may be out of date; verify before outreach.
Most iThome authors publish under a handle and do not state an employer; they sit under 'Employer not identified' and their location is unknown, although the platform is Taiwanese.
Job ads could not be read (Cloudflare). The two Yourator ads come from a fuzzy site search and do not prove dbt use.

Several chapter speakers are listed by first name only (Sam at Dcard, Joshua, Edison, Stephen, Ellen) or by Chinese name only; the assembler cannot match these, so check the past-speaker list before treating a lead as new.
The tier rule raises every emerging voice with 2024+ writing to tier 1, including authors whose posts touch dbt only lightly; read the suggested talk angle before outreach.

LinkedIn: 1 of 69 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 68 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
WiDS Taipei 2024 speakers are listed without talk titles; their evidence links to the overview page.
Employers and dbt wording come from public job ads on 2026-10-01; ads close, so check the employer before outreach.

chapters.label: Tokyo
caveats: Titles, employers and cities come from public pages and Zenn bios, and are often inferred from the employer's Tokyo HQ — verify before outreach.
Many Japanese authors publish under a handle only; names are recorded as written (handle or Japanese name) and ids are ASCII slugs of the handle. Confirm real names before inviting.

Several blog authors are probably past chapter speakers under another name: okiyuki = Motoyuki Oki, Yoshi-ken = Yoshiken, harry/gappy = Harry, sisisin = Shimenyan, t-hiroto = Hiroto Takahashi, ryosuke839 = Ryosuke Lin Yamamoto, 栁澤 @i_125 (Qiita: Satoko Yanagisawa) = 'Yoshiko Yanagisawa'. These were left out to avoid duplicates; the last one suggests the chapter file may misspell her first name.
No women-in-data community source yielded candidates, and gender was never inferred. The organiser should ask the chapter hosts and Snowflake Data Heroes for introductions to balance the line-up.
No job postings were collected: the web-search budget ran out before the job-ad searches.
Only public professional information is recorded; no contact details. Pronouns only when self-stated (none found).

LinkedIn: 4 of 126 people have a profile url, taken word for word from search results. 122 were never searched (linkedin_confidence 'not_searched'); the 2026-10-01 pass searched the best-ranked leads with no known location first.
Speakers from women-in-data community events are recorded by where they spoke (sourced_via women_in_data_community). No one's gender is recorded or inferred.
Most Snowflake女子会 organisers publish under a handle; names are recorded as written, with the handle.
Job ads were read on 2026-10-01. Ads close, so check the link before quoting one.
